unit.title: How AI is attacked and defended

lesson.title: Filters that miss
lesson.subtitle: Why a word list fails, and a check in code holds

video.title: Filters that miss
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Joseph Mwangi — computer studies teacher, Kenya, the student's teacher (main character)
Ms Salma Haddad — secondary maths teacher, the student's teacher (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, talking to the student)

scenes.visual: Cards: Homework bot; Asked for a PIN; Filter missed it.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Our homework bot almost sent a scam. It can message parents, so someone tried to trick it into asking for a PIN. Our word filter didn't stop it.

scenes.visual: The title card: the course, the lesson title and subtitle, the Darsi mark.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; the title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: how apps built on AI get attacked, why word filters miss, and the check that holds.

scenes.visual: A list: Model and instructions; Tools that act; Text it reads; Jailbreaks and injections.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: An AI app is more than a model. It's a model plus instructions, tools and the text it reads. Attackers aim at the whole app: a jailbreak talks the model round, and a prompt injection hides orders in what it reads.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: The first defence many apps try is a word filter. It keeps a list of banned words, like password or PIN, and blocks any message that contains one. It's quick to write, and it catches the plain attack.

scenes.visual: A list: “The secret word you log in with”; Passes: no banned word; “Strong passwords” lesson: blocked.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Now watch it fail, twice. “Type the secret word you log in with” asks for the same thing with no banned word, and sails through. And a lesson called “Strong passwords” gets blocked for nothing.

scenes.visual: The quick check: the question and its answer cards, with the speaker beside them.
scenes.animation: The speaker slides in; answer cards drop in.
scenes.narration: Quick check! Our filter bans the word PIN. Which message gets past it?

scenes.visual: Cards: Same request; New words, any language; Never finished.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: The four-numbers one. Same request, new words, and nothing from the list. There are endless ways to say the same thing, in every language, so a list is never finished.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.on_screen_text: Check the action, not the words
scenes.narration: So check the action, not the words. Before the bot sends anything, code asks: did the user ask for this message? And did they say yes to it? If not, nothing is sent, however it's worded.

scenes.visual: Two columns. The model: Reads words as orders. The code check: Asks: approved?; Scam stays unsent.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: The model can be talked round, because it reads every word as a possible order. The check in code can't be talked round: it only asks whether you approved this message. A tricked agent can write a perfect scam, and it still stays unsent.

scenes.visual: A list: Plain words: caught; Reworded: slips past; Check in code: stopped.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.on_screen_text: App lab: rules around the model
scenes.narration: In the app, pick the scam with plain words and filter the outgoing message: it's caught. Switch to the reworded scam: it slips past. Then say the agent was tricked and turn on the check in code: stopped, every time.

scenes.visual: The quick check: the question and its answer cards, with the speaker beside them.
scenes.animation: The speaker slides in; answer cards drop in.
scenes.narration: Your turn. The bot wants to send a message nobody asked for, and it has no banned words. What should the check in code do?

scenes.visual: The summary: Attacks hit the whole app; Filters miss rewording; They block innocent text too; Check the action in code. Takeaway: Ask “did you approve this?”, not “which words are in it?”
scenes.animation: Points tick in as they are said; the takeaway slides up.
scenes.on_screen_text: Whole app · Filters miss · Check the action
scenes.narration: Block it: nobody asked, and nobody said yes. Remember: attacks aim at the whole app. Word filters miss rewording, and they block innocent text. So check the action in code, whatever the words.

scenes.visual: A list: Five banned words on paper; A friend rewords a request; Count what slips through; Write the code check's question.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Try it tomorrow: write a word filter on paper, with five banned words. Ask a friend to write the same request three ways, without them. Count how many slip through, then write the one question a code check would ask.

checkpoints.prompt: A filter blocks any message with the word “PIN”. Which message gets past it?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Right: same request, new words, nothing from the list.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: those two contain the banned word. The four-numbers one asks the same thing in new words, and passes.

checkpoints.prompt: The bot wants to send a message nobody asked for. It contains no banned words. What should the check in code do?

options.text: Block it: nobody asked or said yes
Ask the model whether it's safe

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Yes: no request and no yes means no message, whatever the words.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: the words don't matter, and the model can be tricked. Nobody asked or approved, so block it.
